solution: Deleting index i can only break the single junction a[i-1], a[i+1]; since values may only be decreased, a[i-1] must stay put and the repair is a cascade to the right. The optimal choice is greedy and maximal: c[i+1] = min(a[i+1], a[i-1]+k) and c[j] = min(a[j], c[j-1]+k) afterwards. Writing d[j] = a[j] - c[j], this becomes d[i+1] = max(0, a[i+1]-a[i-1]-k) and d[j] = max(0, d[j-1] - slack[j]) with slack[j] = k - (a[j]-a[j-1]) >= 0, so the deficit starts at D and is eaten by the running sum of slacks until it reaches zero. With Q[j] = sum of slacks up to j = k*(j-1) - (a[j]-a[1]), which is non-decreasing, the answer is sum over j from i+1 of max(0, D - (Q[j]-Q[i+1])); binary search the last index where that is positive and evaluate the sum with a prefix sum of Q. Total O(n log n) per test (i=1 and i=n always answer 0); the intermediate products need 128-bit or a rebased accumulation since Q can reach 2*10^14. Verified on all seven samples and 20000 random good arrays against a direct per-index greedy.
annotator: claude agent, verified against a brute force
notes: The binary search here is an ordinary search over a monotone prefix-sum array for where the cascading deficit dies, NOT binary-search-answer: there is no feasibility predicate on a guessed answer, so that label was deliberately avoided. The same sum can be done with a monotonic stack or by sorting the queries, but binary search is the natural implementation and matches the judge tag. Judge tag 'data structures' is satisfied by plain prefix sums. Rating is None (contest unrated at extraction time); Div. 3 G. Watch for 64-bit overflow if the prefix sum of Q is multiplied by a length before rebasing.
